meta.rule: beginner wording; every claim is supported by the provenance entry of the same name

tools.name: CalculiX (ccx)
tools.one_liner: Free simulation program by Guido Dhondt and Klaus Wittig. Here it computes the production heat and mechanics results: how hot the package gets, how much it warps, and how hard the solder joints are strained.

tools.name: In-house package-network FV solver
tools.one_liner: Our own Python solver, using SciPy, for how current spreads through the package's power wiring sheet and solder balls. It decides how much current each ball carries.

tools.name: In-house electrical ledger
tools.one_liner: Our own Python bookkeeping of every conductor in the power path: its resistance at its own temperature and the heat it produces, layer by layer.

tools.name: In-house E-T fixed-point driver
tools.one_liner: Our own Python loop: losses heat the package, heat raises resistance, resistance raises losses. It repeats ledger and CalculiX until the numbers settle, then computes warping once.

tools.name: In-house package builders + YAML configs
tools.one_liner: Our own settings files and Python loader that describe the two package designs, Z1 and Z2: layers, materials, converter tiles. The meshes and the electrical ledger are built from them.

tools.name: In-house structured hex mesher (etm.mesh)
tools.one_liner: Our own Python mesher. It cuts each package into small brick-shaped cells that follow every layer and tile edge; the same mesh carries the heat and the warping calculations.

tools.name: Gmsh
tools.one_liner: Free mesh generator by Christophe Geuzaine and Jean-François Remacle. Here it cuts the flat package wiring sheet into small triangles so MOOSE can solve on it.

tools.name: MOOSE heat_transfer module (heat_transfer-opt)
tools.one_liner: Open-source simulation framework, primarily developed by Idaho National Laboratory. Here it is an independent check: it re-solves our heat-flow and current-flow test problems on separate meshes, for comparison.

tools.name: Ansys Electronics Desktop 2026 R1
tools.one_liner: Ansys's commercial platform for electronics simulation. Here it only hosts the Mechanical solver used as a commercial cross-check.

tools.name: AEDT Mechanical (thermal, structural)
tools.one_liner: Ansys's heat and structural solver inside Electronics Desktop. Here it is the commercial cross-check: it re-solves our via, wiring-layer, unit-cell temperature and two-layer bending tests for comparison.

tools.name: PyAEDT (ansys.aedt.core)
tools.one_liner: Python library from Ansys (PyAnsys) that operates Electronics Desktop by script. Here it builds, solves and reads back every Ansys Mechanical check, so each check is a re-runnable script.

tools.name: Closed-form references (in-house)
tools.one_liner: Textbook formulas coded in our Python scripts, such as Timoshenko's formula for how a heated two-layer strip bends, used as a hand-check on CalculiX.

tools.name: Ansys Q3D Extractor
tools.one_liner: Ansys tool that computes resistance, inductance and capacitance of wiring. NOT EXECUTED IN THIS STUDY — LICENSE UNAVAILABLE. Scripts are ready; no Q3D number appears anywhere.
tools.status: NOT EXECUTED IN THIS STUDY — LICENSE UNAVAILABLE

tools.name: Ansys Maxwell (DC conduction)
tools.one_liner: Ansys electromagnetic field solver; its DC current-flow mode was considered as a cross-check. NOT EXECUTED IN THIS STUDY — LICENSE UNAVAILABLE. Ansys Mechanical was used instead.
tools.status: NOT EXECUTED IN THIS STUDY — LICENSE UNAVAILABLE

tools.name: Ansys Icepak
tools.one_liner: Ansys electronics-cooling simulator. Here it re-solves one channel of the cold plate with real water flow (CFD), to check the simple cooling formula the production model uses.

tools.name: Ansys HFSS
tools.one_liner: Ansys high-frequency electromagnetic simulator. NOT EXECUTED IN THIS STUDY. The paper reports an earlier attempt that did not converge; no HFSS number is used.

tools.name: Matplotlib
tools.one_liner: Open-source Python plotting library by the Matplotlib development team. It draws every chart and field picture in the deck from saved results; it draws solver results; it is not the solver.

tools.name: VTK
tools.one_liner: Open-source visualisation toolkit from Kitware. Here it reads MOOSE's result files and renders the RDL field and the re-drawn reference geometry; it draws solver results; it is not the solver.

tools.name: Native SVG via Python
tools.one_liner: Diagrams typed directly in SVG, the W3C standard text format for vector drawings, by our Python scripts, including this map. It draws diagrams; it is not the solver.

tools.name: Reveal.js
tools.one_liner: Open-source web slide framework created by Hakim El Hattab and contributors. This talk is a Reveal.js web page, version 5.1.0, stored inside the repository; it shows slides; it is not the solver.

tools.name: Google Chrome (headless)
tools.one_liner: Google's web browser, run without a window. Here it prints the slide web page into the PDF handout; it draws slides; it is not the solver.

tools.name: rsvg-convert (librsvg)
tools.one_liner: Command-line tool from the GNOME librsvg project that turns SVG drawings into PNG pictures. Here it renders this map for checking; it draws; it is not the solver.

tools.name: pdfLaTeX + BibTeX (TeX Live 2018)
tools.one_liner: Typesetting programs from TeX Live, supported by the TeX Users Group. They build the journal manuscript PDF; they typeset text; they are not solvers.

tools.name: Python (CPython)
tools.one_liner: The programming language, stewarded by the Python Software Foundation, in which all our own code, drivers and figure scripts are written (version 3.12.14).

tools.name: NumPy
tools.one_liner: The basic open-source Python library for arrays of numbers, developed publicly by a community. Every in-house script stores and processes its numbers with it.

tools.name: SciPy
tools.one_liner: Open-source Python library of scientific algorithms. Its sparse equation solver does the number crunching inside our electrical network and ledger codes.

tools.name: ParaView
tools.one_liner: Kitware's open-source visualisation application, built on VTK. NOT INSTALLED here, so not used; VTK, its engine, was used directly to read result files.

tools.name: Graphviz
tools.one_liner: Open-source software that lays out graph diagrams automatically. NOT EXECUTED IN THIS STUDY: installed, but diagrams were written directly as SVG instead.
